questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=2{e}^{2t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x={e}^{2}$ and velocity $v={e}^{2}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 2{e}^{2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{2t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)={e}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & ={e}^{2(1)}+C \\ {e}^{2} & ={e}^{2}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)={e}^{2t}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{2t}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)={e}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1)}+K \\ {e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2\pi $ and velocity $v=4$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\text{d}t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{2})=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ 4 & =2(1)+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+2)\text{d}t \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{2})=2\pi .$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2(\frac{\pi }{2})+K \\ 2\pi  & =-2(0)+\pi +K \\ K & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+2t+\pi .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int -7\,\text{d}t \\  & =-7t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(4)=30.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =-7(4)+C \\ 30 & =-28+C \\ C & =58.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-7t+58.

$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{4})=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+C \\ 0 & =-1+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)+1.

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)={e}^{-2t},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=0$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{-2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{1}{-2}{e}^{0}+C \\ 0 & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{2}.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{2}\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{2}t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{0}+\frac{1}{2}(0)+K \\ 0 & =\frac{1}{4}+K \\ K & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{1}{4}.
$$
